paragraphs: “Why are you learning French words?” Ivan nodded toward the exercise-book lying on the table.
“Why shouldn’t I learn them, sir, to improve my education? I might happen to go some day to those happy parts of Europe myself.”

“Listen, monster.” Ivan’s eyes flashed and he trembled all over. “I’m not afraid of your accusations. You can say what you like about me. And if I don’t beat you to death, it’s only because I suspect you of that crime, and I’ll drag you to justice. I’ll unmask you.”

“In my opinion, sir, you had better keep quiet. What can you accuse me of, when I’m absolutely innocent? And who would believe you? Only, if you begin, I shall tell everything too, for I must defend myself.”
“Do you think I’m afraid of you now?”
“If the court doesn’t believe everything I’ve just said to you, the public will, and you will be ashamed.”
“That’s as much as to say, ‘It’s always worth speaking to a sensible man,’ eh?” Ivan snarled.
“You’ve hit the mark, sir, indeed. And you had better be sensible.”

Ivan got up, shaking all over with indignation, put on his coat, and without answering Smerdyakov any further, without even looking at him, walked quickly out of the cottage. The cool evening air refreshed him. There was a bright moon in the sky. A nightmare of thoughts and sensations filled his soul. “Shall I go at once and inform against Smerdyakov? But what can I tell them? He’s not guilty, anyway. On the contrary, he’ll accuse me. And really, why did I set off for Tchermashnya then? What for? What for?” Ivan asked himself. “Yes, of course, I was expecting something, and he is right....” And for the hundredth time he remembered how, on the last night in his father’s house, he had listened on the stairs. But he remembered it now with such anguish that he stopped dead on the spot, as though he had been stabbed. “Yes, I expected it then, that’s true! I wanted the murder, I did want the murder! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I must kill Smerdyakov! If I don’t dare kill Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!”

Ivan did not go home. He went straight to Katerina Ivanovna and alarmed her by the way he looked. He was like a madman. He repeated all his conversation with Smerdyakov, every syllable of it. However hard she tried to soothe him, he could not be calmed. He kept walking about the room, speaking strangely and without connection. At last he sat down, put his elbows on the table, leaned his head on his hands and said this strange sentence: “If it’s not Dmitri but Smerdyakov who’s the murderer, then I share his guilt, for I put him up to it. Whether I did, I don’t know yet. But if he is the murderer and not Dmitri, then of course I am the murderer too.”

When Katerina Ivanovna heard that, she got up from her seat without a word and went to her writing-table. She opened a box that stood on it, took out a sheet of paper and laid it in front of Ivan. This was the document that Ivan later spoke of to Alyosha as a “conclusive proof” that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna when he was drunk, on the very evening he met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery. That was after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s, when Grushenka had insulted her. Then, parting from Alyosha, Mitya had rushed to Grushenka. I don’t know whether he saw her, but in the evening he was at the “Metropolis,” where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he asked for pen and paper and wrote a document with weighty consequences for himself. It was a wordy, disconnected, frantic letter, a drunken letter in fact. It was like the talk of a drunken man who, on getting home, starts telling his wife or someone in the household, with extraordinary heat, how he has just been insulted, what a rascal insulted him, what a fine fellow he himself is, on the other hand, and how he will pay that scoundrel back. And all that at great length, with great excitement and incoherence, with drunken tears and blows on the table. The letter was written on a dirty piece of ordinary paper of the cheapest kind. The tavern had supplied it, and there were figures scrawled on the back. There was evidently not enough space for his drunken wordiness, and Mitya had not only filled the margins but written the last line right across the rest. The letter ran as follows:

FATAL KATYA: To-morrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! To-morrow I shall try and get it from everyone, and if I can’t borrow it, I give you my word of honor I shall go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I’ll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I’ve been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No, better not forgive me, you’ll be happier and so shall I! Better Siberia than your love, for I love another woman and you got to know her too well to-day, so how can you forgive? I will murder the man who’s robbed me! I’ll leave you all and go to the East so as to see no one again. Not _her_ either, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell! P.S.—I write my curse, but I adore you! I hear it in my heart. One string is left, and it vibrates. Better tear my heart in two! I shall kill myself, but first of all that cur. I shall tear three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though I’ve been a scoundrel to you, I am not a thief! You can expect three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, in pink ribbon. I am not a thief, but I’ll murder my thief. Katya, don’t look disdainful. Dmitri is not a thief! but a murderer! He has murdered his father and ruined himself to hold his ground, rather than endure your pride. And he doesn’t love you. P.P.S.—I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S.—Katya, pray to God that someone will give me the money. Then I shall not be steeped in gore, and if no one does—I shall! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy, D. KARAMAZOV.

When Ivan read this “document,” he was convinced. So it was his brother, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not he, Ivan. In his eyes this letter at once took on the look of a logical proof. There could no longer be the slightest doubt of Mitya’s guilt. It never occurred to Ivan, by the way, that Mitya might have committed the murder together with Smerdyakov. Indeed, such a theory did not fit the facts. Ivan was completely reassured. The next morning he thought of Smerdyakov and his gibes only with contempt. A few days later he actually wondered how he could have been so horribly upset by his suspicions. He resolved to dismiss Smerdyakov with contempt and forget him. So a month went by. He made no further inquiry about Smerdyakov, but twice he happened to hear that the man was very ill and out of his mind.

“He’ll end in madness,” the young doctor Varvinsky said of him, and Ivan remembered this. During the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel very ill. He went to consult the Moscow doctor whom Katerina Ivanovna had sent for just before the trial. And just at that time his relations with Katerina Ivanovna became painfully strained. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna’s “returns” to Mitya, that is, her brief but violent swings of feeling in his favor, drove Ivan into perfect frenzy. Strange to say, until that last scene described above, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna, Ivan had not once in that whole month heard her express a doubt of Mitya’s guilt, in spite of those “returns” that he hated so. It is remarkable, too, that while he felt he hated Mitya more every day, he realized that it was not because of Katya’s “returns” that he hated him, but just _because he was the murderer of his father_. He was aware of this and fully admitted it to himself.

Nevertheless, ten days before the trial he went to see Mitya and proposed a plan of escape—a plan he had obviously thought over for a long time. He was partly driven to this by a sore spot still left in his heart by a phrase of Smerdyakov’s: that it was to his, Ivan’s, advantage for his brother to be convicted, since that would raise his inheritance and Alyosha’s from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He decided to sacrifice thirty thousand on arranging Mitya’s escape. On his way back from seeing him he was very mournful and dispirited. He suddenly began to feel that he was anxious for Mitya’s escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for another reason too. “Is it because I am as much a murderer at heart?” he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride above all suffered cruelly all that month. But of that later....

After his conversation with Alyosha, Ivan suddenly decided, with his hand on the bell of his lodging, to go to Smerdyakov. He was obeying a sudden and peculiar impulse of indignation. He had suddenly remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had only just cried out to him in Alyosha’s presence: “It was you, you, who persuaded me of his” (that is, Mitya’s) “guilt!” Ivan was thunderstruck when he recalled it. He had never once tried to persuade her that Mitya was the murderer. On the contrary, he had suspected himself in her presence, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov. It was _she_, she, who had produced that “document” and proved his brother’s guilt. And now she had suddenly exclaimed: “I’ve been at Smerdyakov’s myself!” When had she been there? Ivan had known nothing of it. So she was not at all so sure of Mitya’s guilt! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with violent anger. He could not understand how, half an hour earlier, he had let those words pass and not cried out at that moment. He let go of the bell and rushed off to Smerdyakov. “This time I may kill him,” he thought on the way.
